text: Somebody signing a renewal ought to be able to find the rule that goes with that lease. That's why I support {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Two neighbors can come up for renewal a day apart. Before we pass {bill-name}, I'd like to know what happens if that day puts them under different rules.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the neighbors sign around the same time, {presiding}, what date would you check to see whether the same limit covers them?
author: Codex writer B

text: When each new term begins, {presiding}. I'd want a tenant to be able to take that date and look up the applicable rule.
author: Codex writer B

text: Get both renewal papers on the table. Under {bill-name} I'd want people checking the start of each term against the dates the limit covers.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask for the start dates, {presiding}. Living across the hall from somebody doesn't tell you that your new lease comes under the same rule.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with the dates on the renewals and the coverage period. My objection to {bill-name} is how much can turn on which side of that line a household falls.
author: Codex writer B

text: A rent roll showing what an owner could charge isn't a stack of paid receipts. I'd pass {bill-name} and hear evidence about what buildings actually collect.
author: Codex writer B

text: The landlord can be owed money on paper and still be short when the fuel bill comes. That's what worries me about {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: The owner brings in a rent roll, {presiding}. Which column would you use to tell how much money actually came in?
author: Codex writer B

text: The payments received, {presiding}. Then I'd compare that with the amounts billed before drawing conclusions about the effect of a limit.
author: Codex writer B

text: Look for collected rent. A lawful maximum tells us something else, and {bill-name} doesn't make a tenant's unpaid balance disappear.
author: Codex writer B

text: Receipts, {presiding}. You can't pay the plumber with the difference between the rent on a ledger and the rent that cleared.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask to see the payment entries. If the page only shows what the owner charged, it won't answer that question about {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Think of the renter whose father owns apartments and has to borrow to keep them up. I favor {bill-name}, and I want both parts of that family's experience heard.
author: Codex writer B

text: You can rent your own place and still worry that a parent's building needs repairs the rent won't cover. I'd take that concern seriously before backing {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you put a renter who helps a parent with a building down as a supporter of {issue} just because they rent?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd put down the position the person actually gives, {presiding}. I support limits myself. That doesn't tell us where another tenant stands.
author: Codex writer B

text: Ask them. They may have a renewal on their kitchen table and a repair estimate on their father's. Let them speak for themselves on {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Their address tells us that they rent, {presiding}. I'd still want to hear what they think the proposal would mean for the building.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd leave that space blank until the renter answers. Being worried about a parent's debt is a reason somebody might oppose {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd give a family some protection at renewal even if the permitted change comes in stages. Knowing when the payment can change is worth something, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Call it a freeze and the family may plan for the same rent through the whole lease. I won't support {bill-name} on a promise that vague.
author: Codex writer B

text: Could we tell a tenant that a freeze at the start of the lease lasts until they move or renew, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Read the schedule first. A lease can begin at the old rent and allow a change partway through. I'd want the dates clear under {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd circle the month the allowance changes, {presiding}. If the freeze covers only the first part of the term, the family needs to know that before signing.
author: Codex writer B

text: Only if the actual rule says so. The word freeze by itself won't tell a tenant how many payments stay the same under {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Show me the end date, {presiding}. A family making a budget needs to know when that protection runs out.
author: Codex writer B

text: An end to stabilization leaves a transition to explain. I'd vote for {bill-name} and make sure the person renewing first can tell when the change reaches them.
author: Codex writer B

text: Neighbors whose leases run out in different months are going to ask one another what to expect. I'd keep stabilization, {presiding}, and give each a rule they can look up.
author: Codex writer B

text: One lease starts before repeal takes effect and the neighbor's starts afterward. Would you give those neighbors the same advice, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep both dates in front of me, {presiding}. Read the transition provision before saying the same rule applies to both households.
author: Codex writer B

text: Find out which renewal each caller has and when the repeal applies. I'd vote to end {issue}, but I won't guess at either person's rent.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask each caller for the new term's start date. An answer that fits the neighbor may be the wrong one under {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Read the two leases separately, {presiding}. I'd sooner keep the protection, but if repeal carries, those families still deserve an answer that fits their own renewal.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for {bill-name}, but nobody should book extra rent as income the morning after repeal. The owner still has to collect it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Letting a landlord ask for more doesn't put more money in a tenant's pocket. I'd keep the limit, {presiding}, and look at the difference between bills sent and payments received.
author: Codex writer B

text: If we end {issue}, can an owner count a higher asking rent as money the building has to spend?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd count it when it's paid, {presiding}. A higher asking rent might never show up in the bank.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want collections beside the billed amount. A vote for {bill-name} can't guarantee that the next rent check clears.
author: Codex writer B

text: A bill mailed out isn't cash coming in. Where would the tenant find the extra money, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Look at what the household paid. If the increase went unpaid, the owner has a balance due and the tenant has a debt. That's my concern about {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: A renter can favor more income for a parent's building and still have qualms about losing protection at home. I'd vote for repeal without putting words in that renter's mouth, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can understand a renter worrying about a parent's repair bills. I'd keep stabilization. Different families can come to that hearing for different reasons, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: A tenant asks for a larger allowed increase to help keep a parent's building going. Does asking for that increase tell us they want to end {issue}?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd record the request for a larger allowance. If we want that person's view on repeal, {presiding}, we'd have to ask another question.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the renter finish. They may want a different increase and still want a limit. My vote for {bill-name} is my own.
author: Codex writer B

text: Asking to change an allowance is a position on its size, {presiding}. Ending the rule altogether is a separate vote.
author: Codex writer B

text: I wouldn't count that testimony as support for {bill-name}. The renter told us about an increase and a parent's costs. Repeal goes further.
author: Codex writer B

text: If we're going to repeal the limit, let's be clear about the lease already in somebody's drawer. I'd want the terms read before anybody sends out a new bill, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Somebody may have signed knowing the rent would stay put at first and change later. I'd vote against {bill-name} rather than leave that household guessing about its next payment.
author: Codex writer B

text: A tenant's lease starts with a freeze and allows a change later on. Could you tell that family what to write on next month's check from the repeal vote alone, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: It takes the lease and the repeal's effective terms to answer that, {presiding}. The vote alone supplies no dollar amount.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask when the frozen period ends and what the agreement says after that. Supporting {bill-name} doesn't give me the figures on that tenant's lease.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd read the lease before telling anybody to pay more, {presiding}. We also need to know when the repeal reaches that agreement.
author: Codex writer B

text: The family should bring in the payment schedule. Which month are they in, {presiding}, and what does the lease say that payment should be?
author: Codex writer B
